newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.Africa sees progress in parastatals revamp.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Africa sees progress in parastatals revamp.

text.p: South Africa said on Monday many of its parastatals now up for privatisation had attractive growth potential despite their legacy of inefficiency and inertia.

Public Enterprises Minister Stella Sigcau said in a speech to parliament that state-owned enterprises, ranging from holiday resorts to arms makers and abattoirs, had in the apartheid years placed priority on ensuring comfortable pensions for their staff.
"In the old order they were used as an area of privilege for only a few," she said. "Some became characterised by a great sense of drift, inertia and lack of direction."

The government had resisted pressure to privatise immediately the concerns -- including telecommunications utility Telkom, air, rail and road carriers grouped in Transnet, and power utility Eskom -- so that it could fully scrutinise and assess them, Sigcau said.
Since her African National Congress took office three years ago, only Telkom has been partly privatised through the sale of a 30 percent strategic equity share to a U.S.-Malaysian consortium.
Last week the government listed pre-qualifiers in the bidding for the regional Sun Air airline.

Sigcau said a strategic equity stake in South African Airways should be sold sometime next year. Most of the remaining parastatals due for partial or full privatisation would be dealt with by the end of this year or early in 1998.
These include the Airports Company Ltd, Alexkor diamond mine, Aventura holiday resorts and forestry concern Safcol.
Sigcau said Safcol, with one of the biggest stockpiles of pruned logs in the world, was among the potential success stories in the state stable.
"This window of opportunity will only remain for a five- to 10-year period before pruned trees reach maturity in other southern hemisphere competitors," Sigcau cautioned.
She said other concerns, notably arms maker Denel and railways operator Spoornet, had a competitive edge due to having been forced into improvisation during the years of anti-apartheid sanctions.
Denel, now under study for restructuring, had potential arms sales of 20 billion rand over the next five years, Sigcau said.

Economists have said privatisation is one of the key measures President Nelson Mandela's government has to take to make a success of its Growth, Employment and Redistribution macroeconomic plan which envisages six percent GDP growth by the year 2000.

Dawie de Villiers, spokesman for the opposition National Party, said in reply to Sigcau's speech that the ANC was split between trying to please foreign investors and trying to appease its domestic constituency which supported a command economy.
"This is well illustrated by the lack of conviction and vision when it comes to privatisation," de Villiers said.
"There are many uncertainties, many questions and few answers. The minister must tackle the issue convincingly and drive privatisation forward with a will."
